# Helping Your Midwife Find You

*A page from the Riverside community midwives, for the families having a home birth with us.*

Congratulations on your pregnancy, and on choosing to have your baby at home. You're about to have one of the best days of your life, and we genuinely cannot wait to be part of it.

This page is about the bit nobody thinks about until it's three in the morning: getting us to your front door, in the dark, in the rain, carrying a mountain of kit, with one woman in labour and a second midwife somewhere behind us on the ring road.

We've written it with jokes, because that's how we'll say it out loud at the booking visit. But everything on here is real and it all matters. Please read it once now, when you're calm, and then stick the checklist on your fridge.

---

## 1. When we can come to you

**Home birth cover starts at 37 weeks.**

From 37 weeks onwards, we can attend your home birth. Before 37 weeks, we can't, and you'd need to go in to the maternity unit instead. We'll say this at your booking visit and we'll say it again at 36 weeks, because everybody forgets it. Everybody. We once had a family pack for the hospital, read the wrong page of the folder, and turned up at their house at 35 weeks with the gas and air cylinders. It was hilarious for us and not at all hilarious for them.

So: **37 weeks is the line.** If you think labour has started before then, phone the birth line and let us talk it through with you. That's what we're there for.

## 2. When labour starts, ring the birth line

**Riverside Birth Line: 0151 XXX XXXX**

This is the number that reaches whichever midwife is on call, day or night. Please use it rather than a personal mobile. Our personal mobiles are for emergencies, and also for Deb'sding of the tea biscuits, but mostly they're for emergencies.

If you're not sure whether you're in labour yet, ring anyway. We would far rather have a call at 2am that turns out to be a false alarm than a call at 2am that turns out to be a baby halfway down the hall.

**A few other things worth knowing:**

- Put the birth line number in your phone now, and write it on the fridge. Don't rely on finding it in a folder at 3am with one hand.
- Keep your phone **charged and on loud**. If we ring you back, pick up.
- If you have a home video or monitor on, you can switch it off when we arrive. No one wants to be filmed before they've had a shower.
- **We come with you if you need to go in.** If at any point you or the baby need hospital care, we travel with you and we stay with you. You're not being abandoned at the door.

## 3. Parking: we need space for two cars

**Two midwives attend your birth**, and we usually come in separate cars. So we need room for **two** cars if you can manage it, ideally not on the same side of the road.

We bring a lot. Gas and air cylinders, the big equipment bag, the birthing pool kit when it's needed, boxes of sterile packs, and enough stuff to run a small clinic. Our arms are tired before we've even said hello.

**If you live in a permit parking area — including parts of Anfield and Kensington — sort it now, not on the day.** You can ask Liverpool City Council for a **visitor permit** for your street, or leave one ready on the dashboard. Yes, we have had tickets. More than one. There's a particular stretch of Anfield where a midwife in a van with a gas cylinder in the back is a very unusual thing for the wardens to see, and it does not help our case.

If a permit isn't possible, then just make sure there's a space free and tell us on the night. We'd much rather know in advance than circle your block at 4am.

## 4. Making your house findable (the important bit, honestly)

Liverpool has wonderful, distinct, deeply confusing streets, and sat nav is not always on our side. Here is what we've learned the hard way, on your behalf:

**Have your house number clearly visible and lit.** Not "it's the third one past the newsagent". The actual number, on the gate, on the door, big enough to read from a moving car at night.

**If your house has a name as well as a number, tell us the number.** We once spent twenty minutes driving round a block of flats in Everton because Flat 14 was not next to Flat 13 — it was in a different building, the other side of the courtyard, facing a car park. The dad eventually gave up and waved a tea towel out of the window, and that, we must stress, is what saved us.

**If your address has no number at all** — we have in mind a lovely terraced house called *Rosemary Cottage*, a street of houses all named something romantic, none of them numbered — then we need a landmark. The nearest bus stop, the shop, the church, the pub with the green door. Sat nav sent us to a chippy once. The chippy was very helpful, but we still hadn't found you.

**Put your porch light on.** Please. In winter, in the dark, with drizzle, every street on the Wirral looks identical, and the one house with a light on is the one with the baby in it. If the bulb's gone, a torch on the step or a lamp in the window does the same job. This is the single most helpful thing you can do.

**Balloons on the gate.** A family did this for us and we found them in under a minute. It was the best idea anyone has ever had. We are fully prepared to become the team that turns up to every house with balloons on the gate. Please, more people should do this.

**Check the gate, the buzzer, and the path.** If the gate is locked, if the buzzer doesn't work, or if there's a step we can't see in the dark, ring us. We'd rather be told than stood at in the gate at 3am.

## 5. Getting through the door

Once we're outside, we need to get in, and we need to get in with a lot of kit.

- **Leave a key with us, or leave the door unlocked, or have someone awake.** If nobody answers the door, ring the birth line and we'll keep trying.
- **Clear the path from the door to the room you'll be in.** Hallway, stairs, landing. Shoes off, coats off, the washing basket moved, the shoe rack moved, the Runner laid down if you have one.
- **No Lego.** We know. You built the house, or the children built it, and it is not ours to judge. But please put it in a box, because a footful of Lego at 4am is a genuine hazard and it is nearly always the small pieces.
- **Towels on the rail.** A clean towel, a stack if you can. We will use them. So will you.
- **Torches.** One in the hallway, one in the room you plan to use.
- **Move the furniture you want to move, before labour starts.** A sofa pushed back to make space takes two minutes in the calm and twenty in the contractions.

## 6. The pets

We love dogs. Genuinely, we love dogs. One of our team has a staffie called **Pippin** who is besotted with everybody and who has to be shut in another room on every visit, because he loves us *too much*, and because a dog who is thrilled to see you is not a dog who is being careful around a new baby.

So please: **give the dog or cat another room, with water, before we arrive**, and keep them there through the birth. It isn't that we don't want to meet them. It's that nobody, human or otherwise, should be jumping on us while we're working. Pippin would like to be clear that he feels maligned.

## 7. What3words, or a pin on WhatsApp

Both are good. Use whichever you already use, and send it **to the birth line phone**, so it comes to whoever is on call.

**What3words** gives us three words like *shelves.legs.hotel* which pin your front door to the earth. **A WhatsApp pin** dropped on your gate or doorstep works just as well and takes about ten seconds.

Send it early in the day if you can — the day before, say — so we can test it. We have had a what3words code that led us confidently to a completely different house, and it turned out the code had been copied from a group chat of somebody else's. Send it again on the day and tell us it's updated. **We will check the pin before we set off**, and if it doesn't match where we're standing, we will ring you. That's fine. Ring us.

## 8. What we are like

In the Philippines, people say a midwife is like family. That's how we think of it too.

We are coming into your home to help you have your baby. We'll be calm, we'll be quick, we'll probably cry a bit (that's us, not you), and we'll tell you what we see as we go. You're in charge of your birth, we're in charge of keeping you and your baby safe, and those two things fit together better than most people expect.

If something is going wrong, we'll tell you plainly. If you're frightened, tell us. Nobody has ever been in trouble for being frightened.

---

## The Fridge Checklist

*Print this, stick it on the fridge, and tick it off as you go. Yes, we mean physically on the fridge.*

**Before 37 weeks**
- ☐ Home birth cover starts at 37 weeks — before that, maternity unit
- ☐ Birth line number saved in my phone: 0151 XXX XXXX
- ☐ Birth line number written on this fridge

**Getting us there**
- ☐ House number visible from the road and lit at night
- ☐ Porch light working, or torch by the door
- ☐ Gate code / buzzer tested
- ☐ Two parking spaces kept clear
- ☐ Visitor permit applied for (Anfield, Kensington and other permit areas) or permit on the dashboard
- ☐ What3words or WhatsApp pin sent to the birth line
- ☐ Landmark given if there's no house number ("the house with the green gate", "next to the shop")

**Getting us in**
- ☐ Key left out, or door unlocked, or someone awake
- ☐ Hallway and stairs clear
- ☐ Shoes, coats, washing basket, shoes off at the bottom of the stairs
- ☐ Lego in a box
- ☐ Clean towels on the rail
- ☐ Torches: hallway and birth room
- ☐ Furniture moved
- ☐ Birth room chosen and aired

**On the day**
- ☐ Phone charged and on loud
- ☐ Birth line called
- ☐ Bin bags, water, snacks for me and the other midwife (we will absolutely accept a biscuit)
- ☐ Kettle on
- ☐ Pet in another room, with water
- ☐ Family and neighbours told, so nobody rings the bell at 4am

---

*Send us your what3words the day before. Ring the birth line, not a personal mobile. And put the porch light on.*

**Riverside Community Midwives**

---

*Two things to fill in before this goes out: the birth line number in the header, in section 2 and on the checklist, and the team's contact details at the foot of the page. Worth adding a line at the end of section 2 saying "the same number is on the front of your welcome folder" so people can find it. If you want a Facebook-friendly version, this drops into a post almost as it is, with the checklist as a photo of the fridge.*
